components.text: Explain what objective oughtness is and how it arises within a materialist account rather than from emotion.
Explain what objective oughtness consists in and how it arises rather than merely naming goodness.
Identify the nature and source of objective evaluative truth within a materialist ontology.
Explain why moral evaluation is cognitive and fact-related rather than merely an emotional expression.
Identify what objective goodness is within a materialist account and explain its source.
Address the claim that ethical statements express emotion rather than truth-apt factual cognition.
Show that life's vulnerability and preservation are necessary for evaluative and ethical concepts.
Show that life-supporting guidance exhausts the practical role of ethical oughts for volitional agents.
Show that life's mortality and preservation requirements are necessary for evaluative and ethical concepts.
Show that life-supporting guidance exhausts ethical relevance for volitional agents.
Explain how actor-centered life-supporting guidance condemns conduct that does not harm the actor's survival or preferences.
Show that life's status as value foundation supplies standards regarding another living creature's suffering.
Explain how actor-centered life-supporting oughts condemn gratuitous animal torture that does not impair the actor's survival.
Explain the normative significance of animal life within the proposed factual foundation of value.
Explain why gratuitous animal torture is wrong despite lacking an obvious survival cost to the torturer.
Explain why gratuitous animal torture is wrong when it does not threaten the torturer's immediate survival.
Use contempt for life to justify why gratuitous destruction and animal abuse are immoral.
Establish life as the value-conferring foundation without assuming that life is already valuable.
Derive animal-abuse wrongness from contempt for life without assuming life's disputed moral value.
Establish life's status as value-giving rather than presupposing that status in its applications.
Show that the life-based account assumes life's intrinsic value when explaining the origin of evaluation.
Explain how normative guidance arises without positing an intrinsic entity or property called goodness.
Explain how life grounds valuation without presupposing that life is intrinsically morally valuable.
Explain the source and logical status of life-based oughts.
Show that a pre-moral choice to live can establish objective rather than merely conditional normative authority.
Establish that life-serving guidance binds agents beyond their antecedent nonobjective commitment to living.
Show how a pre-moral choice to live can yield objective rather than merely conditional normativity.
Explain how a life-based standard generates objective principles extending beyond an individual's conditional choice.
Explain how an actor-centered ethic can recognize constraints concerning other living beings.
Explain how life-based principles extend beyond one chooser to universal interpersonal constraints.
Provide a non-intrinsic route from human-life requirements to moral principles.
Show why another person's rights bind an actor when violating them genuinely advances the actor's own flourishing.
Show that choosing one's own life generates constraints protecting another person's life.
Show why another person's rights constrain an actor whose own life genuinely benefits from murder.
Derive individual rights from life requirements rather than assuming the disputed moral status of other persons.
Explain why an egoist's choice of personal life creates reasons to respect another person's rights.
Derive another person's rights from rational egoism without presupposing the disputed moral constraint.
Explain what rights are and why their constraints arise from human life rather than being presupposed moral properties.
Explain why force remains impermissible when a particular violator might personally benefit from it.
Explain what rights are and why they matter within a life-based rational-egoist framework.
Explain why force and murder remain prohibited even when a violator claims personal benefit.
Explain why emotional expression does not exhaust moral cognition or determine moral truth.
Identify a non-emotional route for knowing good, bad, right, and wrong.
Address the emotivist claim that moral judgments are expressions of emotion rather than cognitive knowledge.
Identify the cognitive route by which moral goodness is understood.
Show whether emotional mechanisms can explain stable moral concern without functioning as instruments of factual knowledge.
Explain differential moral concern for animals without deriving it from a universal life standard.
Explain practical moral boundaries without objective rights or rational-egoist derivation.
Explain moral-pattern differences without treating rational cognition as identifying objective moral facts.
Explain differential emotional concern for animals and other living beings.
Test the life standard as a standard of flourishing and full human functioning rather than mere avoidance of death.
Clarify what 'life' denotes in the value standard before assessing whether its use is circular.
Explain why flourishing supplies objective authority rather than merely elaborating a chosen end.
Clarify the content of the life standard whose action-guiding and objective status is disputed.
Explain whether the standard concerns mere avoidance of death or richer human functioning.
Specify flourishing rather than immediate survival as the relevant actor-centered standard.
Show that human flourishing adequately captures the content ordinarily expressed by moral goodness.
Explain how actor-centered human life captures familiar concern for other people.
Explain how the proposed standard captures familiar moral concern for animals.
Show that human flourishing adequately captures the meaning and domain of moral goodness.
Show that the proposed definition captures familiar concern for other persons.
Show that the definition captures familiar moral concern for animals.
Explain how the account distinguishes concern for animal life from specifically human moral status and rights.
Provide a rational rather than purely emotive account of differing moral treatment across species.
Explain why animals can matter without possessing human rights.
Explain animal-value boundaries through principled distinctions rather than emotional resemblance alone.
Clarify why valuing animal life does not entail treating animals as human moral agents or rights holders.
Address the claimed omission of animals from the life-based account.
